name.text: Instantaneous rate of change on a falling graph

questiontext.text:
The graph below falls continuously from a height of \( y = {@ya@} \) at \( x = {@xa@} \) down to a height of \( y = {@yb@} \) at \( x = {@xb@} \). The point on the graph where \( x = {@c@} \) is marked in red.

generalfeedback.text:
The big idea. The instantaneous rate of change of a function at a point is the slope of the tangent line to its graph at that point: how steeply, and in which direction, the graph is heading at that exact point. A graph that falls as x increases has tangents that slope downward, so its rate of change is negative. Here the red point is at \( x = {@c@} \).

You ticked the statement about a zero rate. A rate of zero needs a horizontal tangent (a peak, a trough or a level stretch); here the graph is falling.
You left out a correct statement: the graph is falling at the marked point, so the rate there is negative.
You left out a correct statement: the instantaneous rate of change at a point is the slope of the tangent line at that point.
You left out a correct statement: the graph keeps falling across the interval, so the rate is negative at every interior point.
You left out a correct statement: the instantaneous rate is the value the average rates settle to as the step shrinks.

You left out a correct steepness comparison: compare how steep the tangents are at the two points.
You left out a correct statement: for this graph (a straight line) the instantaneous rate equals the average rate everywhere.
You left out a correct comparison with the average rate: compare the tangent's slope at the point with the chord's slope.
You left out a correct statement: this graph is a straight line, so its rate is the same at every point.

falsefeedback.text: More than one statement is classified wrongly. Think of the tangent at the marked point: which way does it slope, and how does its steepness compare with the other tangent and with the chord joining the ends?

truefeedback.text: You ticked the statement about a positive speed. The rate of change keeps its sign: a falling graph has a negative rate. The speed is the size of the rate without the sign.
You ticked the statement about the end points. The end points give only the average rate over the whole interval; the instantaneous rate at a point is the slope of the tangent at that point.
You ticked a steepness comparison that is not correct for this graph. Compare how steep the tangents are at the two points, ignoring the heights.
You ticked a steepness comparison that is not correct for this graph. Compare how steep the tangents are at the two points, ignoring the heights.

You ticked the statement about the average rate. The average rate over the whole interval comes from the chord joining the ends; the instantaneous rate at a point is the slope of the tangent there, and for this graph the two differ.
You ticked a comparison with the average rate that is not correct for this graph. Compare the slope of the tangent at the point with the slope of the chord joining the two ends.
You ticked the statement that the rate is the same everywhere. This graph curves, so its steepness (and therefore its instantaneous rate) changes from point to point.
